items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026
items.q: The Foundation was founded by a few jazz enthusiasts including Billy Taylor and Herb Storfer, Bill Wurtzel and a few really – you know Sandy Jordan, which was Clifford Jordan’s wife, and I hope I’m not leaving out too many people but Jimmy Owens

ctx.x: Wow. In New York City. You were the only person, huh?

Yes. They advertised it in Psychology Today, which I don't know why, maybe it was all they could afford, but they offered me fifty big ones and I was very excited, I was a single parent. I had another part time job that I did besides the train station blues and when I left they called me back all week until the job at the Jazz Foundation said, “We want you back, we’ll start you at a hundred thousand.” And that was huge money back then. That was huge money to me you know, twenty years ago, whatever. And I could…

Was there a sort of, I’m going to use the word “triage” when a person was presented or came to you or was brought to the organization, was there an assessment like what do we need immediately and what could be the long-term plan for this person.

items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I know Bob Cranshaw and Jimmy Owens were finding people who really needed it, because they were all active musicians on the road.

ctx.x: Tell us, and give us some of the history of how the Jazz Foundation of America reached the point where you became its steward.

Well, it’s all very beautiful. These were people who just love jazz, and they were all involved with the museum. A few things had happened, and the space was taken away, and they really didn’t know what to do. They gave everything to the Schomberg. But then they said, “Why don’t we become an organization to keep jazz alive and to archive it, to promote it?” I think for a couple of years, it sort of went along like that. I know they did an event at Town Hall which helped them raise some money. And then, Jamil…

house, and he’d pull it out and say, “Ok, here’s a month’s rent. You had a heart attack; you’re going to be off the road for two months—we’ll cover it.” Which I think is so fantastic. Then Dizzy ended up with cancer at Englewood Hospital, and his doctor was the saint, Dr. Frank Forte. He asked him... I wish we could interview Frank right now, because he’s so important to what we do, and he tells it so beautifully.
